title: Where should you store JWT in the browser — HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie (safest) vs localStorage (vulnerable to XSS) vs sessionStorage — and why?
shortTitle: Where to Store JWT in the Browser (HttpOnly Cookie vs localStorage vs sessionStorage)

s1_definition.profdef: The safest place to store a JWT in a browser is an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie: HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript so cross-site scripting cannot read it, Secure forces it over HTTPS only, and SameSite blocks it from being sent on cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF. Storing the token in localStorage or sessionStorage makes it readable by any JavaScript on the page, so a single XSS flaw lets an attacker steal the token; localStorage persists across tabs and restarts, while sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes. The trade-off is that cookies are automatically attached and therefore need CSRF protection, which the SameSite attribute largely provides.
s1_definition.analogy: Storing a JWT in localStorage is like leaving Rajesh's cheque book on the open counter of National Bank of India — any clerk (any script) passing by can grab it. Storing it in an HttpOnly cookie is like keeping the cheque book in a sealed drawer that only the bank's own back-office machinery can open; the counter staff and visitors cannot reach inside. The sealed drawer is safer, but because it opens automatically for every transaction, the bank adds a second check (SameSite and CSRF tokens) so a trickster cannot make the drawer open for the wrong request.
s1_definition.oneliner: Prefer an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so JavaScript cannot steal the token; localStorage is one XSS away from losing everything.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The safest place to store a JWT in a browser is an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie: HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript so cross-site scripting cannot read it, Secure forces it over HTTPS only, and SameSite blocks it from being sent on cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF. Storing the token in localStorage or sessionStorage makes it readable by any JavaScript on the page, so a single XSS flaw lets an attacker steal the token; localStorage persists across tabs and restarts, while sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes. The trade-off is that cookies are automatically attached and therefore need CSRF protection, which the SameSite attribute largely provides.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Storing a JWT in localStorage is like leaving Rajesh's cheque book on the open counter of National Bank of India — any clerk (any script) passing by can grab it. Storing it in an HttpOnly cookie is like keeping the cheque book in a sealed drawer that only the bank's own back-office machinery can open; the counter staff and visitors cannot reach inside. The sealed drawer is safer, but because it opens automatically for every transaction, the bank adds a second check (SameSite and CSRF tokens) so a trickster cannot make the drawer open for the wrong request.

**One line to remember:** Prefer an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so JavaScript cannot steal the token; localStorage is one XSS away from losing everything.

sections.s2_technical:
localStorage and sessionStorage are plain JavaScript-accessible key-value stores. Reading the token is as easy as `localStorage.getItem("jwt")`, which means any injected script — from a compromised dependency, a bad ad, or a reflected XSS — can read and exfiltrate it. localStorage persists until explicitly cleared and is shared across tabs; sessionStorage is scoped to one tab and cleared on close, slightly reducing exposure time but not the XSS risk itself. Because these require the app to manually attach the token, they are immune to CSRF, but that is a weak consolation against the much more common XSS.

An HttpOnly cookie is set by the server with `Set-Cookie: jwt=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/`. HttpOnly means `document.cookie` cannot see it, so even a successful XSS cannot read the token directly. Secure means it is only sent over HTTPS. SameSite=Strict (or Lax) means the browser will not attach it to requests originating from other sites, which blocks the classic CSRF money-transfer attack. The cookie is sent automatically, so the server reads it without any client code.

The senior nuance: HttpOnly cookies are the recommended default for web apps, combined with SameSite plus, for sensitive state-changing endpoints, an anti-CSRF token for defense in depth. For pure APIs consumed by native mobile apps, tokens live in the platform secure storage (Keychain or Keystore), not a browser at all. A common anti-pattern is putting a long-lived token in localStorage "for convenience"; in banking that is unacceptable because one XSS equals full account takeover. If a framework forces header-based tokens, keep the access token in memory only (a JavaScript variable, lost on refresh) and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India web app loads a third-party charting script that turns out to be compromised and runs attacker JavaScript. If Rajesh's JWT sits in localStorage, that script reads it in one line and sends it to the attacker, who now controls his account. This is exactly why JavaScript-readable storage is dangerous — XSS equals token theft.

Problem 2 — The bank instead stores the token in an HttpOnly cookie, so the same malicious script cannot read it. But cookies are sent automatically, so a malicious site could try to trick the browser into firing a transfer. This is exactly why we add SameSite and a CSRF token — to stop the automatic cookie from being abused on cross-site requests.

Our mini-project simulates both storage strategies: a `TokenStorage` interface with a `LocalStorageStrategy` (readable by scripts) and an `HttpOnlyCookieStrategy` (not readable by scripts). The demo shows a simulated XSS script successfully stealing from localStorage and failing against the HttpOnly cookie, then shows SameSite blocking a cross-site send.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

javac BrowserStorageDemo.java
java com.bank.storage.BrowserStorageDemo

# Spring Boot — server sets the hardened cookie
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/jwt-browser-storage-service-1.0.0.jar
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's JWT and a simulated malicious XSS script running on the page.

Step 1: The token is stored with `LocalStorageStrategy`. Its `readableByJavaScript` returns the token, modeling how `localStorage.getItem` exposes it to any script.

Step 2: The `XssScript` calls `trySteal`, which simply reads what JavaScript can read, and successfully obtains the token. In a real app it would exfiltrate it to the attacker's server — full account takeover from one injected script.

Step 3: The token is stored with `HttpOnlyCookieStrategy`. Its `readableByJavaScript` returns null, modeling the browser hiding an HttpOnly cookie from `document.cookie`. The same XSS script now gets nothing — theft fails.

Step 4: Finally the demo checks `wouldSendOnCrossSiteRequest`, which returns false, modeling SameSite=Strict refusing to attach the cookie to cross-site requests. This blocks the CSRF path that would otherwise exploit the automatically-sent cookie. The combination — unreadable by JS and not sent cross-site — is why the hardened cookie is the safest choice.

```text
2026-10-31 23:05:00.010 SEVERE  [BrowserStorageDemo] localStorage: XSS STOLE the token -> account takeover: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.rajesh.sig
2026-10-31 23:05:00.012 INFO    [BrowserStorageDemo] HttpOnly cookie: XSS could NOT read the token -> safe from theft
2026-10-31 23:05:00.013 INFO    [BrowserStorageDemo] HttpOnly cookie sent on cross-site request? false (SameSite=Strict blocks CSRF)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Server login response
    │
    ├─ Option A: body → JS stores in localStorage
    │      │
    │      ▼
    │   malicious script: localStorage.getItem('jwt') STOLEN (XSS)
    │
    └─ Option B: Set-Cookie: jwt=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict
           │
           ▼
        malicious script: document.cookie  → token NOT present (safe)
           │
           ├─ same-site request → cookie auto-sent
           └─ cross-site request → SameSite=Strict blocks it (CSRF stopped)
```

```text
  │LocalStorageStrategy│ │ HttpOnlyCookieStrategy    │

  Decision matrix:
    localStorage   : persists, XSS-readable            → avoid for tokens
    sessionStorage : per-tab, still XSS-readable        → still risky
    HttpOnly cookie: JS cannot read + Secure + SameSite → SAFEST (default)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The safest place to keep a JWT in a browser is an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. HttpOnly means JavaScript cannot read the cookie through document.cookie, so even a successful cross-site scripting attack cannot steal the token. Secure means the cookie only travels over HTTPS. SameSite, set to Strict or Lax, means the browser will not attach the cookie to requests that originate from other sites, which blocks the classic CSRF attack. Storing the token in localStorage or sessionStorage instead makes it readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS flaw hands the attacker the token.

In my banking project this distinction is critical because the blast radius of a stolen token is full account access. In my demo I modeled both approaches: with localStorage a simulated malicious script read the token in one line, which in the real world means account takeover, while with the HttpOnly cookie the same script got nothing because the browser hides it from JavaScript.

The trade-off I always mention is that cookies are sent automatically, which is convenient but opens CSRF. We close that with SameSite, which refuses to send the cookie on cross-site requests, and for sensitive state-changing endpoints we add an anti-CSRF token for defense in depth. localStorage avoids CSRF because the app attaches the token manually, but that is a poor consolation because XSS is far more common and far more damaging.

So my default recommendation for a banking web app is HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies with CSRF protection on write endpoints. If an architecture forces header-based tokens, I keep the access token only in a JavaScript variable in memory, which is lost on refresh and never persisted, and keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie. For native mobile apps I store tokens in the platform secure storage like Keychain or Keystore rather than any browser mechanism at all.

---

keyPoints: JWT: Header.Payload.Signature — Base64 encoded, not encrypted
Signature verifies integrity — payload is readable by anyone
Access token: short-lived (15 min). Refresh token: long-lived (days)
Store in HttpOnly cookie (XSS-safe), never in localStorage
